exactBefore.body:
## Chef's Note

Sautéing bacon first, removing it for garnish, then cooking aromatics in the rendered fat infuses this soup with smoky umami backbone. Including a Granny Smith apple prevents the squash from becoming overly sweet - the apple's acidity balances the soup's natural sugars and provides brightness within the puree itself.

## Directions

Use an electric pressure cooker with a sauté setting. Follow the model’s minimum-liquid requirements and soup fill limit before sealing; do not exceed its marked limit. Use full natural pressure release for this soup. The 12-minute pressure timer excludes coming to pressure and releasing it; both vary with the cooker and load, so the listed 45 minutes is not a ready-to-serve deadline.

1.  **The Render:** Set the electric pressure cooker to "Sauté" (High). Add diced bacon and cook until crispy (6-8 mins). Remove bacon to a plate, leaving the fat in the pot.
2.  **Aromatics:** Add onion to the bacon fat. Sauté for 3 minutes until translucent. Stir in garlic, sage, and thyme; cook for 30-45 seconds until fragrant.
3.  **Pressure:** Stir in the squash, carrots, celery, and chopped apple. Pour in the chicken stock and season with salt and pepper.
4.  **Cook:** Secure the lid. Set to **High Pressure for 12 minutes**.
5.  **Release:** Turn Keep Warm off and allow pressure to release fully naturally. Open only when the cooker indicates no pressure remains and its instructions permit opening. Remove and discard the thyme sprigs.
6.  **The Emulsion:** Stir in the heavy cream. With the cooker off, use an immersion blender according to its hot-liquid instructions. Keep the blade guard submerged, start on low, and stop the motor before lifting it out. Puree until smooth.
7.  **Serve:** Ladle into bowls. Garnish with the reserved crispy bacon and chives for the mandatory **Textural Snap**.

learning.timing: Plan roughly 60–100 minutes elapsed for one cooker load, with about 25–35 minutes active work. ## Chef's Note

Crisp bacon supplies both the cooking fat and the garnish. Softening onion, sage and garlic in that rendered fat gives the squash soup a smoky, savory base; a Granny Smith apple adds acidity inside the purée. Add the full heavy-cream amount after pressure cooking, then keep the bacon crisp by adding it at service.

## Directions

1. **Render the bacon:** Have the prepared vegetables ready and choose cooker loads before heating. Use a Cuisinart CPC-600 with its clean cooking pot, fitted sealing ring and unobstructed pressure valves. Keep the combined food and liquid at or below 60% of the pot’s capacity and never above its marked limit. At larger scales, divide every ingredient proportionally into complete cooker loads before starting; each soup load must contain at least ½ cup of the listed stock or broth. Repeat the whole cooking process for each load. Do not multiply the pressure timer. Select Browning with MENU and press START. Add slices of bacon and cook, stirring, until brown and crisp, about 6–8 minutes. Transfer the bacon to a plate for garnish and leave all its rendered fat in the pot.
2. **Soften the onion:** Press START/CANCEL to stop Browning, then select Sauté with MENU and press START. Add medium sweet onion to the bacon fat and cook, stirring, for about 2–3 minutes, until translucent.
3. **Add the herbs and garlic:** Stir in garlic cloves, sage leaves, and sprigs of fresh thyme and cook about 30–60 seconds, until fragrant without burning.
4. **Add the vegetables and stock:** Add Granny Smith apple, butternut squash, large carrots, stalk of celery, chicken stock, and kosher salt and black pepper. Stir thoroughly and use a wooden or silicone spoon to loosen any browned bits from the bottom without scratching the pot. Keep the apple and squash in pieces until after pressure cooking; do not add the cream yet. Check the total food-and-liquid fill before sealing.
5. **Pressure-cook until soft:** Press START/CANCEL to stop Sauté, and wait 2–3 minutes for the inner pot to cool slightly. Fit and lock the lid, set the pressure-limit valve to its closed • position, select High Pressure with MENU, set TIME to 12 minutes, then press START/CANCEL. The countdown starts only after pressure has built. Do not count pressure buildup as part of those 12 minutes.
6. **Release fully naturally:** When the timer finishes, leave the CPC-600 on its automatic Keep Warm setting while pressure falls fully naturally. Wait until the red float is completely down and the lid unlocks; this commonly takes 12–30 minutes and can take longer. Then press START/CANCEL to turn off and open the lid away from your face. Do not force the lid or release steam manually for this recipe. Remove and discard the thyme sprigs. Test the squash and carrots: a fork should pass through easily. If firm, select Simmer with the lid off and cook until soft before blending.
7. **Finish and blend:** Turn off and unplug the cooker. Stir in heavy cream. Use an immersion blender that is suitable for hot liquids, protect the nonstick pot, keep its blade guard submerged and stop the motor before lifting it out. Blend until smooth, then taste and adjust seasoning.
8. **Serve with the crisp garnish:** Ladle the soup into bowls. Add fresh chives and the reserved crisp bacon. The creamy purée and crisp bacon should stay distinct until serving.

originalCooking.name: Instant Pot Butternut Squash Soup
originalCooking.ingredients:
4 slices bacon, diced
1/2 medium sweet onion, diced
3 cloves garlic, minced
4 sage leaves, minced
3 sprigs fresh thyme
1 (2 1/2 pound) butternut squash, peeled, seeded, and cubed
3 large carrots, cut into 1-inch pieces
1 stalk celery, cut into 1-inch pieces
1 Granny Smith apple, cored and chopped
4 cups chicken stock
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste
1/3 cup heavy cream
2 tablespoons chopped fresh chives
originalCooking.directions:
Set 6-qt Instant Pot® to the high saute setting. Add bacon and cook until brown and crispy, about 6-8 minutes. Transfer to a paper towel-lined plate.

Add onion, and cook, stirring frequently, until translucent, about 2-3 minutes. Stir in garlic, sage and thyme until fragrant, about 1 minute.

## Chef's Note

Sautéing bacon first, removing it for garnish, then cooking aromatics in the rendered fat infuses this soup with smoky umami backbone. Including a Granny Smith apple prevents the squash from becoming overly sweet - the apple's acidity balances the soup's natural sugars and provides brightness within the puree itself.

## Directions

Use an electric pressure cooker with a sauté setting. Follow the model’s minimum-liquid requirements and soup fill limit before sealing; do not exceed its marked limit. Use full natural pressure release for this soup. The 12-minute pressure timer excludes coming to pressure and releasing it; both vary with the cooker and load, so the listed 45 minutes is not a ready-to-serve deadline.

1.  **The Render:** Set the electric pressure cooker to "Sauté" (High). Add diced bacon and cook until crispy (6-8 mins). Remove bacon to a plate, leaving the fat in the pot.
2.  **Aromatics:** Add onion to the bacon fat. Sauté for 3 minutes until translucent. Stir in garlic, sage, and thyme; cook for 30-45 seconds until fragrant.
3.  **Pressure:** Stir in the squash, carrots, celery, and chopped apple. Pour in the chicken stock and season with salt and pepper.
4.  **Cook:** Secure the lid. Set to **High Pressure for 12 minutes**.
5.  **Release:** Turn Keep Warm off and allow pressure to release fully naturally. Open only when the cooker indicates no pressure remains and its instructions permit opening. Remove and discard the thyme sprigs.
6.  **The Emulsion:** Stir in the heavy cream. With the cooker off, use an immersion blender according to its hot-liquid instructions. Keep the blade guard submerged, start on low, and stop the motor before lifting it out. Puree until smooth.
7.  **Serve:** Ladle into bowls. Garnish with the reserved crispy bacon and chives for the mandatory **Textural Snap**.

## Chef's Note

Adapted from Sandy Clifton's potato-leek soup at Simply Happy Foodie, this version softens leeks in butter and oil before adding flour and broth. White pepper and nutmeg bridge the gap between earthy potatoes and rich cream, classic French seasonings for potato-leek soup.

## Directions

Use an electric pressure cooker with a sauté setting. Follow its minimum-liquid, maximum-fill and pressure-release instructions; these depend on the model.

1.  **The Sweat:** Set electric pressure cooker to "Sauté." Add butter and olive oil. Once hot, add leeks and sauté for 5-7 minutes, stirring, until softened; reduce the heat if the leeks start to brown.
2.  **Aromatics:** Add garlic and sauté for 30 seconds. Sprinkle the flour over the leeks and stir for 1 minute to cook out the raw starch taste.
3.  **Deglaze:** Pour in the broth slowly, scraping the bottom of the pot to ensure no flour sticks.
4.  **Pressure:** Add potatoes, bay leaf, nutmeg, salt, and pepper. Secure the lid. Set to **High Pressure for 7 minutes**.
5.  **Release:** Turn Keep Warm off and let pressure release fully naturally. Open only after the pressure indicator has dropped and the model’s instructions confirm it is safe.
6.  **The Emulsion:** Remove the bay leaf. With the heat off, use an immersion blender with its head submerged to puree the soup. Stop once smooth; prolonged blending can make potato soup gluey.
7.  **Finish:** Stir in the half-and-half. Taste and adjust salt if needed.
8.  **Serve:** Garnish with a dollop of sour cream and fresh chives for **Textural Balance**.

## Cooking Notes

The original saved recipe was adapted from the contributor’s grandfather’s recipe.

## Timing

Allow about 70 minutes including preparation, sautéing, the cooker coming to pressure, seven minutes at pressure, full natural release and finishing. Pressure buildup and natural release vary with the cooker and batch size and may take longer; they are not included in the seven-minute pressure setting. Wash sliced leeks thoroughly to remove grit before measuring.

## Chef's Note

Sandy Clifton’s potato-leek soup softens leeks in the full butter and olive oil, then disperses a small flour addition into plenty of broth. Add the dairy after pressure cooking, and stop blending when the potatoes are smooth to keep the soup creamy rather than gluey. White pepper and optional nutmeg complement the potatoes and cream.

## Directions

1. **Soften the leeks:** Use a Cuisinart CPC-600 with its clean cooking pot, fitted sealing ring and unobstructed pressure valves. Keep the combined food and liquid at or below 60% of the pot’s capacity and never above its marked limit. At larger scales, divide every ingredient proportionally into complete cooker loads before starting; each soup load must contain at least ½ cup of the listed stock or broth. Repeat the whole cooking process for each load. Do not multiply the pressure timer. Select Sauté with MENU and press START. Add unsalted butter, extra-virgin olive oil, and leeks. Cook, stirring, for about 5–7 minutes or until the leeks soften; a little color is fine, but stop and lower to Simmer if they begin to catch.
2. **Add garlic and flour:** Use garlic cloves and all-purpose flour: stir in the garlic and cook about 30 seconds until fragrant. Sprinkle in the flour and stir for 1 minute, coating the leeks without leaving dry clumps.
3. **Dissolve the flour in broth:** Pour in chicken broth or vegetable broth gradually while stirring. Scrape the entire pot bottom with a wooden or silicone spoon so no flour or browned leek residue remains stuck. The mixture should be a loose broth with vegetables, not a thick paste.
4. **Add potatoes and seasoning:** Stir in Yukon Gold potatoes, fresh bay leaf, nutmeg (if using), and salt and white pepper. Check total food-and-liquid fill before closing the lid. Keep the dairy and garnish out of the pressure stage.
5. **Pressure-cook:** Press START/CANCEL to stop Sauté, and wait 2–3 minutes for the inner pot to cool slightly. Fit and lock the lid, set the pressure-limit valve to its closed • position, select High Pressure with MENU, set TIME to 7 minutes, then press START/CANCEL. The countdown starts only after pressure has built.
6. **Release fully naturally:** When the timer finishes, leave the CPC-600 on its automatic Keep Warm setting while pressure falls fully naturally. Wait until the red float is completely down and the lid unlocks; this commonly takes 12–30 minutes and can take longer. Then press START/CANCEL to turn off and open the lid away from your face. Do not force the lid or release steam manually for this recipe. Remove and discard the bay leaf. A fork should pass easily through the potato cubes; if they remain firm, select Simmer with the lid off until soft.
7. **Blend just until smooth:** Turn off and unplug the cooker. Use an immersion blender suitable for hot liquids, keep its head submerged, protect the nonstick pot and stop its motor before lifting. Stop once the soup is smooth; prolonged blending can make potato soup gluey. Alternatively, use a countertop blender that permits hot liquids, following its venting and hot-fill instructions and blending carefully in small batches.
8. **Add the dairy:** Stir in half-and-half after blending. Taste and adjust seasoning. If reheating for service, warm gently while stirring rather than reducing the finished cream soup hard.
9. **Garnish and serve:** Add sour cream and chopped fresh chives or parsley to each serving. Serve hot, or divide into shallow containers and chill promptly under refrigeration for chilled service.

## Cooking Notes

Sandy Clifton adapted the soup from her grandfather’s recipe. Serve it hot or chilled.

originalCooking.ingredients:
1/2 cup hoisin sauce
1/4 cup soy sauce
1 tablespoon unsulfured molasses
3 1/2 tablespoons coarsely chopped peeled fresh ginger
6 garlic cloves
3/4 cup honey
1 tablespoon sambal oelek or Chinese chile-garlic sauce
2 racks pork spareribs or baby back ribs (4 pounds), halved lengthwise
originalCooking.directions:
In a blender, combine the hoisin sauce with the soy sauce, molasses, ginger, garlic and 1/2 cup of the honey and puree until smooth. Add the sambal oelek and pulse to combine.

Cut the spareribs into 3-rib sections and transfer to a pressure cooker. Add the hoisin puree and let stand, turning the ribs occasionally, for 45 minutes.

Add 1/4 cup of water to the cooker. Cover and cook at high pressure for 20 minutes.

Line a rimmed baking sheet with foil. Run cold water over the pressure cooker to release the pressure. Transfer the ribs to the prepared baking sheet, meaty side up. Boil the cooking juices until reduced to 2 cups, about 5 minutes. Transfer the hoisin pan sauce to a bowl.

Preheat the broiler and position a rack 8 inches from the heat. Brush the ribs all over with the remaining 1/4 cup of honey and broil, turning once, until the ribs are glazed and browned, about 5 minutes. Transfer the rib sections to a cutting board and slice them into individual ribs. Serve the ribs with the hoisin pan sauce.

## Chef's Note

Honey-glazed spareribs are a Chinese-American restaurant staple. This version uses a pressure cooker to achieve fall-off-the-bone tenderness in 20 minutes instead of hours of smoking or braising. The hoisin-ginger cooking liquid gets boiled down into a concentrated syrupy glaze, then brushed on the ribs before broiling for sticky, caramelized edges. A major time-saver with restaurant-quality results.

## Directions

1.  **Puree:** In a blender, combine hoisin, soy, molasses, ginger, garlic, and 1/2 cup of the honey. Blend until smooth.
2.  **Pressurize:** Place the ribs in a pressure cooker. Pour the puree over the ribs. Add 1/4 cup water.
3.  **Cook:** Seal and cook on **HIGH PRESSURE** for 20 minutes.
4.  **The Reduction:** Allow pressure to release fully naturally, following the cooker instructions. Open only after its indicator confirms no remaining pressure and its instructions permit opening. Transfer the ribs to a foil-lined baking sheet, meaty side up. Pour the liquid from the cooker into a saucepan and boil over high heat for 10 minutes until reduced by half.
5.  **The Lacquer:** Brush the ribs generously with the reduced sauce and the remaining 1/4 cup honey.
6.  **Char:** Broil 6 inches from the heat for 3-5 minutes until the glaze is bubbling and charred at the edges.
7.  **Serve:** Sliced into individual ribs with extra sauce on the side.

## Chef's Note

Honey, hoisin, molasses, ginger, garlic and chile give these ribs a full sweet-savory glaze. For the Cuisinart CPC-600, drain the thick marinade before pressure cooking the ribs above a separate thin liquid, then boil and reduce every bit of marinade with the cooking juices. Broiling concentrates the sticky coating; check tenderness before that dry finish.

## Directions

1. **Blend the marinade:** Use hoisin sauce, soy sauce, unsulfured molasses, fresh ginger, garlic cloves, sambal oelek or Chinese chile-garlic sauce, and 2/3 of the honey. Set aside the remaining one third of the listed honey in a clean container for the broiler finish. Blend the hoisin, soy, molasses, ginger, garlic and marinade honey until smooth, then pulse in the chile sauce so it is fully included.
2. **Marinate under refrigeration:** Put pork spareribs or baby back ribs in a covered food-safe container, add all the blended marinade and refrigerate for 45 minutes, turning occasionally. Ask the butcher to halve the racks lengthwise if needed to make the sections fit safely in the cooker. The rib size and thickness affect tenderness.
3. **Keep the pressure liquid thin:** Use a Cuisinart CPC-600 with a suitable pressure-cooker rack that holds the ribs above the liquid. Drain the ribs thoroughly over the marinade container, scrape off excess thick sauce, and keep all this raw-contact marinade covered in the refrigerator until the reduction stage. Add water to the clean cooker pot, place the rack over it and arrange the drained ribs on the rack. Do not pour the thick marinade into the pressure liquid. Keep food and liquid at or below 60% of the pot’s capacity and never above its marked limit; use additional complete loads if needed. The 1-cup water allowance applies separately to every load and does not scale down with the recipe.
4. **Pressure-cook the ribs:** Fit the lid, lock it, set the pressure-limit valve to the closed • position and select High Pressure with MENU. Set TIME to 25 minutes and press START/CANCEL. This is a starting cook; the countdown begins only once pressure has built. Check tenderness after full natural release.
5. **Release fully naturally:** When the timer finishes, leave the CPC-600 on its automatic Keep Warm setting while pressure falls fully naturally. Wait until the red float is completely down and the lid unlocks; this commonly takes 12–30 minutes and can take longer. Then press START/CANCEL to turn off and open the lid away from your face. Do not force the lid or release steam manually for this recipe.
6. **Check tenderness before glazing:** Test a meaty section away from the bone. The meat should be easy to pierce and the bones should move readily; the pressure timer alone does not promise this. If still firm, remove the rack, return ribs to the cooking liquid and select Simmer with the lid off, turning occasionally, until tender. Keep liquid in the pot during this finishing stage, adding water only as needed to prevent it from drying out. Check the meat reaches at least 145°F / 63°C, away from bone. Transfer tender ribs to a foil-lined rimmed baking sheet and retain all cooking juices.
7. **Cook and reduce the full sauce:** Pour all the cooker juices and all reserved raw-contact marinade into a saucepan. Bring the entire sauce to a full boil, stirring, and keep it boiling for several minutes before it touches cooked meat or is served. Then reduce, stirring frequently, until glossy and thick enough to coat a spoon; use its consistency rather than a fixed final cup volume. All the hoisin, soy, molasses, ginger, garlic, chile and marinade honey stay in this sauce. Extra cooker loads add liquid and can extend reduction.
8. **Brush the ribs:** Preheat the broiler and position the rack about 6–8 inches from its heat, as the broiler permits. Use 1/3 of the honey. Brush the ribs with the fully boiled reduced sauce and the reserved clean honey. Keep serving sauce separate from the brush and working glaze. The original serving alternative is to brush with the reserved honey alone and serve all the cooked hoisin sauce alongside.
9. **Broil and serve:** Broil until the coating bubbles and browns at the edges, starting checks at 3 minutes; about 3–5 minutes is a guide, and different broilers vary. Turn once carefully and watch closely so the honey browns without burning. Confirm at least 145°F / 63°C in a meaty section away from bone, then rest at least 3 minutes before cutting into individual ribs and serving with the clean serving sauce.

## Cooking Notes

Grated ginger distributes through the sauce. For a coarsely chopped ginger preparation, blend it until smooth and use 3½ tbsp in the original 4-lb rib batch, adjusting that proportion at other scales. Baby back ribs and Chinese chile-garlic sauce are alternatives. For a honey-only coating, brush the ribs with the reserved honey and serve the fully cooked hoisin sauce alongside.
